newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.N. agency pleads for North Korean baby food.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency pleads for North Korean baby food.

text.p: The World Food Programme (WFP) on Friday launched an international appeal for $95 million to feed hungry babies and toddlers in North Korea.
Catherine Bertini, WFP Executive Director, told a news coneference in Seoul the U.N. agency had more than doubled its earlier appeal for $41 million.
The extra money would go to nurseries and kindergartens for children aged under six, who accounted for 2.6 million out of a population of 23 million.
"The additional food aid, almost exclusively, will be directed to children under six, and we will proceed to send food to every nursery and kindergarten throughout the country," she said.
Bertini, who toured North Korea last month, said many children in nurseries she visited showed signs of malnutrition. Some had orange-tinted hair, bloated stomachs and limbs.
She showed video footage of children with blank gazes.
Bertini said most North Koreans were surviving on 100 grammes (3.5 ounces) of rice or maize per day and supplemented their diets with leaves or roots.
"We visited people in their homes and saw almost no protein source -- no meat, no fish -- and saw empty cupboards and a very limited amount of food," she said.
Unless emergency food aid arrived soon "by summer large-scale malnutrition and deaths" would occur.
Bertini said the impoverished Stalinist state needed 2.3 million tonnes of grain to stave off famine.
Pyongyang officials had told her by late March or April the country would run out of food. They asked that limited funds be used to buy maize rather than more expensive rice.
Bertini, who leaves Seoul on Saturday after a three-day visit, said she had appealed to South Korean leaders to increase their original pledge of $6 million.
The National Unification Ministry said in a statement it would consider the new request.
The United States pledged $10 million to the original appeal.
